explanations.explanation: Right there in the opening line: "Give thanks to the LORD, for He is good…" (Psalm 107:1) The psalm starts with goodness before it tells a single story. I love that, friend. Everything after it is the proof.

Mighty sounds like a solid reason, and I'd have picked it too on a rushed day. But it isn't the one this verse gives. The line says, "…for He is good…" The psalm saves the rest of the evidence for the pictures that come after.

Holy is a fine word, but it isn't what this opening line says. The verse says, "…for He is good; His loving devotion endures forever." So the first reason is His goodness. That's the one the whole psalm builds on.

That's not what the verse says, friend. It says His loving devotion "endures forever." There's no deserving clause tucked in the fine print. I've burned plenty of batches in my day, and "forever" still means forever.

Right, it's false. The psalm says His loving devotion "endures forever." (Psalm 107:1) Nothing in that line sets a limit or asks anyone to earn it. It just keeps going, and that's good news for every one of us.

That's it. The psalm says the LORD redeemed them "…from the hand of the enemy" (Psalm 107:2). Redeemed is the word the psalm uses for them. Anybody who's come through a tough spot can lift a hand on that one.

I see why that one tempts you, but it isn't in this verse. Here the redeemed are brought out "…from the hand of the enemy" The psalm uses a different picture to make the point. It's the enemy's hand that He pulls them out of.

That's a picture from another passage, friend, not this one. The fiery furnace is in Daniel 3:20. Verse 2 here says He redeemed them "…from the hand of the enemy" and there's no furnace anywhere in this psalm. Stay with that enemy's hand, because that's what the redeemed got out of.

Not quite, friend. The psalm says He gathered them "…from the lands, from east and west, from north and south." (Psalm 107:3) That's four directions, not one corner of the map. So many places, and He reaches every one of them.

Right, it's false. He gathered them "…from the lands, from east and west, from north and south." (Psalm 107:3) That's every direction on the compass. No spot on the map is too far for Him to gather someone from.
Yes. The wanderers are in desert wastelands, "…finding no path to a city in which to dwell." (Psalm 107:4) They have somewhere to get to, but no way to get there. That's a hard spot to be in.

It's the other way around, friend. The psalm says they were "…finding no path to a city in which to dwell." (Psalm 107:4) They're out in the wastelands with no road to a place to live. That's the trouble they're about to cry out about.

Yes, they "…cried out to the LORD in their trouble…" (Psalm 107:6) They don't wait until things get better first. They cry out right in the middle of the trouble. And the psalm says He delivered them from their distress.

That isn't what the verse says. It says, "Then they cried out to the LORD in their trouble…" (Psalm 107:6) Idols never show up in this scene. The cry goes to the LORD, and He's the one who delivers them.
No king in this scene, friend. The psalm says, "Then they cried out to the LORD in their trouble…" (Psalm 107:6) The cry goes to the LORD, and the delivering comes from Him too.

You got it, baker. The verse says, "He led them on a straight path to reach a city where they could live." (Psalm 107:7) Earlier they were finding no path to a city, and now He leads them on a straight one. That's quite a change from wandering the wastelands.

I get the guess, since deserts can feel like one big loop. But the verse says He led them on a straight path. (Psalm 107:7) They went from no path to a straight one. That's about as good as directions get.

Hidden isn't what the verse says, friend. It says He led them on a straight path to reach a city where they could live. (Psalm 107:7) The wanderers were finding no path, and now He's the one leading them. A straight path, and a city at the end of it.

True. The psalm says, "For He satisfies the thirsty and fills the hungry with good things." (Psalm 107:9) Hungry and thirsty is exactly how those wanderers started out. Now the psalm says why thanks is in order.

It's actually true, friend. Verse 9 says, "For He satisfies the thirsty and fills the hungry with good things." That's the reason behind the thanks. The same hunger and thirst from the desert, now filled.

The psalm says the opposite. These prisoners were there "…because they rebelled against the words of God and despised the counsel of the Most High." (Psalm 107:11) So going against God is exactly how it describes them. The psalm doesn't soften it, and it doesn't stop there either.

Right, it's false. The prisoners were in affliction and chains "…because they rebelled against the words of God and despised the counsel of the Most High." (Psalm 107:11) That's the reason the text gives. The good news is still ahead, because the LORD answers their cry.
That's the one. He "…broke away their chains." (Psalm 107:14) Broken away, not loosened or trimmed. Those chains don't get a second chance.
Lighter chains are still chains, friend. The psalm says He "…broke away their chains." (Psalm 107:14) He doesn't just adjust them. He breaks them away.

I once shared a drawer with a key that never found its door, so I know keys get a lot of credit. But this verse doesn't mention one. It says He "…broke away their chains." (Psalm 107:14) He does the work Himself.

Yes. "For He has broken down the gates of bronze and cut through the bars of iron." (Psalm 107:16) Bronze gates and iron bars are about as locked as it gets. And He goes through both. That's the reason given this time for the thanks line in verse 15.

That's a famous wall, but it's not in this psalm. Verse 16 says He "…has broken down the gates of bronze and cut through the bars of iron." Prison gates and bars are the picture here. Keep your eyes on the bronze.

Good try, but no temple pillars in this verse, friend. It says He "…has broken down the gates of bronze and cut through the bars of iron." (Psalm 107:16) Those are gates and bars, the kind that hold prisoners in. The LORD breaks through them.

True. "They loathed all food and drew near to the gates of death." (Psalm 107:18) Loathed is a strong word for how they felt about food. I think that tells you how serious things were. It's a heavy moment, and the next verse brings the turn.

It's true, friend. The psalm says, "They loathed all food and drew near to the gates of death." (Psalm 107:18) Loathed is a strong word, and the psalm picked it on purpose. It's a heavy moment, and the next verse brings the turn.
Yes, "…the gates of death." (Psalm 107:18) They drew near to it. And the very next verse shows where they turn: they cried out to the LORD (Psalm 107:19).
A city did show up earlier in this psalm, so I see the mix-up. But these folks "…drew near to the gates of death." (Psalm 107:18) That's a very different gate. It shows how serious their trouble is.

I get the guess, friend, since gates and temples go together in a lot of minds. But the psalm says they "…drew near to the gates of death." (Psalm 107:18) Drew near, and then in the next verse they cry out and He saves them. That's why the cry in verse 19 matters so much.

You got it, baker. The verse says, "He sent forth His word and healed them; He rescued them from the Pit." (Psalm 107:20) His word is what He sends, and the healing comes with it. The same verse says He rescued them from the Pit.
A prophet isn't in this verse, friend. It says, "He sent forth His word and healed them…" (Psalm 107:20) The word itself goes out and the healing happens. He also rescued them from the Pit.
Bread isn't what the psalm says, friend. It says, "He sent forth His word and healed them…" (Psalm 107:20) His word is what He sends. The same verse says He rescued them from the Pit.

explanations.answer: Offer sacrifices and tell His works
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker. The psalm says, "Let them offer sacrifices of thanksgiving and declare His works with rejoicing." (Psalm 107:22) Sacrifices and telling His works go together there. The thanks gets said out loud, and with joy.

explanations.answer: Fast and keep it to themselves
explanations.explanation: Keeping quiet is the opposite of what the psalm says. It says, "Let them offer sacrifices of thanksgiving and declare His works with rejoicing." (Psalm 107:22) Declare means say it out loud. And rejoicing is part of it.

Silent doesn't fit this verse at all, friend. The healed are told to "…offer sacrifices of thanksgiving and declare His works with rejoicing." (Psalm 107:22) That's telling people, and doing it happily. So go with the version that has some noise in it.
Yes, "…His wonders in the deep." (Psalm 107:24) These traders are out on the mighty waters, and they see what the LORD does there. The deep is where those wonders show up. Plenty to look at.

The desert was the first picture, so I see why it came to mind. But this time we're at sea, and the verse says "…His wonders in the deep." (Psalm 107:24) The traders are on the mighty waters. The deep is what they see.

A city came up earlier in the psalm, but not in this verse. The traders "…saw the works of the LORD, and His wonders in the deep." (Psalm 107:24) They're out on the mighty waters, doing trade. The deep is where the wonders are.

That's the one. "For He spoke and raised a tempest that lifted the waves of the sea." (Psalm 107:25) A tempest is a big storm, and the psalm says it comes at His word. That's why it counts among the wonders out there.
Locusts aren't in this scene, friend. The psalm says, "…He spoke and raised a tempest that lifted the waves of the sea." (Psalm 107:25) We're out on the water, and the tempest is the wonder here.
No army in this verse, friend. It says, "…He spoke and raised a tempest that lifted the waves of the sea." (Psalm 107:25) A tempest is a big storm. It's the one that lifts the waves.

The psalm says the opposite. In the storm, "…all their skill was useless." (Psalm 107:27) These are traders who know ships, and their know-how doesn't help. I think that's exactly why they cry out in the next verse.
Right, it's false. The psalm says "…all their skill was useless." (Psalm 107:27) They reel and stagger, and their skill gets them nowhere. Then they cry out to the LORD, and He brings them out.

Yes. "He calmed the storm to a whisper, and the waves of the sea were hushed." (Psalm 107:29) From a tempest to a whisper, and the waves go quiet. That's a big change. The next verse says they rejoiced in the silence (Psalm 107:30).

Splitting the sea belongs to a different story, friend. In Exodus 14:21 the waters were divided. In this psalm, "He calmed the storm to a whisper, and the waves of the sea were hushed." (Psalm 107:29) Hushed, not split.
Frozen waves aren't in this psalm. The verse says, "He calmed the storm to a whisper, and the waves of the sea were hushed." (Psalm 107:29) Hushed, not frozen. It goes from loud to a whisper.
Yes, "They rejoiced in the silence…" (Psalm 107:30) After all that noise, quiet is the thing that makes them glad. And then He guides them to the harbor they wanted.
Trembling fits the storm, not the silence. During the tempest their courage melted. But once the waves are hushed, "They rejoiced in the silence…" (Psalm 107:30)

I see why weeping came to mind after a storm like that. But the psalm says, "They rejoiced in the silence…" (Psalm 107:30) The waves are hushed, and they're glad. No tears are mentioned in this verse.

You got it, baker. The verse says, "Let them exalt Him in the assembly of the people and praise Him in the council of the elders." (Psalm 107:32) Both the gathering of the people and the council of the elders are named. The psalm calls for praise out in the open.

Priests and Levites aren't mentioned here, friend. The verse says, "Let them exalt Him in the assembly of the people and praise Him in the council of the elders." (Psalm 107:32) That's the people and the elders.

No king shows up in this verse. It says, "Let them exalt Him in the assembly of the people and praise Him in the council of the elders." (Psalm 107:32) Out in the open, with the people and the elders. That's where the sailors are told to speak up.
Yes. He turns fruitful land into fields of salt "…because of the wickedness of its dwellers." (Psalm 107:34) The psalm names the reason right there. Nothing is left to guess about.

That's a nice thought, but the psalm gives a different reason. It says fruitful land becomes fields of salt "…because of the wickedness of its dwellers." (Psalm 107:34) The reason is the people's wickedness.
No army in this verse, friend. It says the fruitful land becomes fields of salt "…because of the wickedness of its dwellers." (Psalm 107:34) The psalm gives the people's wickedness as the reason.

You got it, baker. The verse says, "He turns a desert into pools of water and a dry land into flowing springs." (Psalm 107:35) Verse 33 says He turns rivers into deserts, and this one goes the other direction. Dry land becomes flowing springs.

It's true, friend. Verse 35 says, "He turns a desert into pools of water and a dry land into flowing springs." The same LORD who turns rivers into deserts in verse 33 does this one too. Dry ground doesn't get the last word here.

That's the opposite of what the verse says, friend. "He blesses them, and they multiply greatly; He does not let their herds diminish." (Psalm 107:38) The herds are not dwindling. The blessing includes them.

Right, it's false. "He blesses them, and they multiply greatly; He does not let their herds diminish." (Psalm 107:38) The people multiply greatly, and He does not let the herds diminish. The blessing covers the herds too.
Yes. He "…pours out contempt on the nobles and makes them wander in a trackless wasteland." (Psalm 107:40) A trackless wasteland means no path to follow. That's quite a turn for nobles.
Prison was in an earlier picture, so I see the mix-up. But for the nobles, the verse says He "…makes them wander in a trackless wasteland." (Psalm 107:40) There's no trail out there to follow.

No plague in this verse, friend. It says He "…pours out contempt on the nobles and makes them wander in a trackless wasteland." (Psalm 107:40) The picture is wandering with no trail. That's what He does to them.

You got it, baker. The verse says, "But He lifts the needy from affliction and increases their families like flocks." (Psalm 107:41) The needy get lifted from affliction, and their families increase like flocks. It's a good contrast with the nobles in the verse before.

The nobles are in the verse before this one, and it doesn't go well for them. This verse turns the other way: "But He lifts the needy from affliction and increases their families like flocks." (Psalm 107:41) The needy are the ones He lifts.

The proud aren't named in this verse, friend. It says, "But He lifts the needy from affliction and increases their families like flocks." (Psalm 107:41) The needy are the ones getting lifted, and their families grow like flocks.
Nope, they don't mourn. "The upright see and rejoice…" (Psalm 107:42) What they see makes them glad. Rejoicing is the response.
Right, it's false. The psalm says, "The upright see and rejoice…" (Psalm 107:42) They watch what the LORD has done, and they're glad. Mourning isn't what this verse says.

That's the one. "Let him who is wise pay heed to these things and consider the loving devotion of the LORD." (Psalm 107:43) The psalm ends by pointing to the wise. And what they're told to consider is His loving devotion.
Strong isn't the word the psalm lands on, friend. It says, "Let him who is wise pay heed to these things…" (Psalm 107:43) The wise are the ones called to pay attention.

Rich isn't in this line. The last verse says, "Let him who is wise pay heed to these things and consider the loving devotion of the LORD." (Psalm 107:43) The wise are called to pay heed. That's who the psalm ends with.
